blocks.text: **Bronchiectasis** is **permanent, abnormal widening of the bronchi**. Whatever the trigger, the end state is the same: **chronic suppurative infection** of the airways, daily purulent sputum, and steadily progressive scarring and loss of lung. It may involve a single lobe or be widespread through both lungs.

Think of it as a **vicious circle**: neutrophil-driven inflammation and repeated infection damage the airway wall, the damaged airway clears mucus even less well, and retained mucus feeds the next infection. Breaking the circle (clearance + infection control) is the logic of treatment.

blocks.title: Pathology
items: Dilated airway walls are destroyed and chronically inflamed; the lining of the cavities may be **granulation tissue, squamous epithelium or ordinary ciliated epithelium**.
Cilia are lost or work poorly, so secretions pool and mucus plugs form; the damaged airways become collapsible.
The **bronchial arteries hypertrophy** — this is why bleeding in bronchiectasis can be brisk or even catastrophic.
The surrounding lung becomes inflamed and fibrotic; in advanced disease normal architecture is progressively destroyed.

blocks.title: Symptoms
rows: Present every day, chronic and persistent
Large daily volumes, persistently purulent (yellow/green), thick and foul-smelling in severe disease
Blood streaking is common; bigger bleeds with infective exacerbations; occasionally massive
When infection reaches the pleura or a segment collapses behind retained secretions
More sputum, more purulence, fever, malaise, anorexia
Weight loss, anorexia, exertional breathlessness, wheeze

blocks.title: Signs
items: **Coarse crackles** over the affected area (often the bases) when the dilated airways contain sputum.
**Finger clubbing** — especially in cystic fibrosis.
Locally reduced breath sounds if a proximal bronchus is plugged and the lobe collapses.
Bronchial breathing over heavily scarred lung in advanced disease; wheeze and inspiratory "squeaks" may also be heard.
Signs may be unilateral or bilateral.

blocks.text: A **normal chest examination does not exclude bronchiectasis**: if the dilated airways are empty of secretions and there is no collapse, there may be no physical signs at all.

Haemoptysis **plus finger clubbing** should make you think of **lung cancer or bronchiectasis** first. Chronic suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema, CF) is a major group of clubbing causes.

blocks.note: Look at: finger clubbing from the front and side — loss of the angle at the nail bed and increased nail curvature.

blocks.text: Two broad routes lead to bronchiectasis: an **inborn defect** of airway ion transport or ciliary function (for example cystic fibrosis), or **acquired damage** to the bronchi from a destructive infection, an inhaled toxin or a foreign body. Either way, chronic airway inflammation and infection follow. Even after full work-up, a cause is found in only **about half** of patients.

**Tuberculosis is the commonest cause of bronchiectasis worldwide** (Davidson and Kumar agree). In children, severe early infection — **whooping cough, measles**, primary TB — is the classic acquired trigger.

blocks.title: Causes grouped by mechanism
rows: Cystic fibrosis; primary ciliary dyskinesia, including **Kartagener syndrome** (sinusitis + situs inversus/dextrocardia)
Suppurative or aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary TB, non-tuberculous mycobacteria
Primary hypogammaglobulinaemia, selective IgA or IgG2 deficiency; secondary — HIV, malignancy
**ABPA** (complicating asthma or CF), after lung transplant, graft-versus-host disease
Inhaled foreign body (e.g. peanut), bronchial tumour, enlarged tuberculous hilar nodes, inspissated mucus, post-TB stenosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren, SLE, ANCA vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
COPD (association increasingly recognised), sarcoidosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

blocks.text: Source clash: a US review book (Step-Up) calls **cystic fibrosis the commonest cause**, accounting for half of cases. Davidson and Kumar state that **TB is the leading cause worldwide**, and Kumar treats CF bronchiectasis as a largely separate entity. For this course follow Davidson: **TB worldwide**.

blocks.title: Cystic fibrosis — exam essentials
items: **Autosomal recessive**; carrier rate about **1 in 25**, incidence about **1 in 2500** live births in white populations.
Gene on the **long arm of chromosome 7** encodes **CFTR**, an apical chloride channel; commonest mutation **ΔF508**, with more than 2000 mutations described.

Faulty CFTR → less chloride secretion and loss of the brake on epithelial sodium channels → **excess sodium and water absorption** → dehydrated airway surface liquid → infection, ciliary dysfunction and bronchiectasis.

Lungs are normal at birth; **Staph. aureus** dominates in childhood, then in adulthood many are colonised by **P. aeruginosa**, S. maltophilia or other Gram-negative organisms; resistant strains (including Burkholderia cepacia) are a later problem.
Bronchiectasis begins in the **upper lobes** and later spreads through both lungs.
Most men are infertile because the **vas deferens fails to develop**.

blocks.note: Look at: normal versus CF airway cell — absent/defective apical CFTR chloride channel, unchecked sodium channel, water drawn out of the airway lining.

blocks.text: **Lady Windermere syndrome**: non-tuberculous mycobacterial (MAC) infection with bronchiectasis of the **right middle lobe and lingula** in older women who habitually suppress their cough.

Do not mix up the two "sinusitis + chest" syndromes: **Kartagener** = primary ciliary dyskinesia **with situs inversus**; **Young** = acquired clearance defect with **azoospermia** and normal anatomy.
Investigation has four aims: **confirm** the diagnosis, **find the underlying cause**, identify **reversible factors**, and look for **complications**.

blocks.title: Confirming the diagnosis
rows: Thick-walled, dilated airways that fail to taper ("tram tracks"); a bronchus wider than its companion artery (**signet ring sign**); cysts at bronchial ends, mostly lower lobes
Often **normal** unless disease is gross; later tram-track lines, ring shadows, cysts (sometimes with fluid), consolidation or collapse
Needed at exacerbations and repeatedly: H. influenzae, Staph. aureus, **P. aeruginosa**; also Aspergillus and mycobacteria (extended/NTM culture must be requested)
Obstructive pattern with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio

blocks.title: Finding the cause
rows: **Sweat test + CFTR genotyping** — for **all patients under 40**, and at any age if suspicion is high
**Nasal nitric oxide** (very low); **saccharin test** (should be tasted within 20 min, much longer in ciliary dysfunction); nasal biopsy for ciliary beat frequency and electron microscopy
Serum IgG, IgA, IgM (± IgG subclasses) and antibody responses to Hib, tetanus and pneumococcal vaccines
Total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE or skin-prick test, eosinophil count, Aspergillus precipitins
Alpha-1 antitrypsin level; colonoscopy if IBD suspected

blocks.text: A **normal chest X-ray does not rule out bronchiectasis** — CT is far more sensitive and is required whenever the history fits.
Diagnosis of CF in practice: clinical picture + **sweat electrolytes + genotype**. UK newborn screening uses **immunoreactive trypsin** plus genetic testing of a blood spot.

blocks.note: Look at: CT with widely dilated, thick-walled bronchi in both lower lobes.
Look at: each thick-walled bronchus is larger than the artery beside it — the signet ring appearance.

blocks.text: Treatment rests on four pillars: **airway clearance**, **anti-inflammatory therapy**, **treatment of infection**, and **treatment of complications**. Treat any underlying cause, and if there is airflow obstruction add inhaled bronchodilators and inhaled glucocorticoids.

blocks.title: Airway clearance (daily, for life)
items: **Postural drainage** — lie so that the affected lobe is uppermost.
**Active cycle of breathing**: deep breaths, then forced expirations (huffs), then a strong cough to clear what has moved up.
Positive expiratory pressure mask, or oscillating devices (flutter, Acapella); autogenic drainage; chest percussion.
At least **5–10 minutes twice a day** for most patients; more during exacerbations.
**Nebulised hypertonic saline** acts as a mucoactive agent.

blocks.title: Antibiotics
rows: COPD-type antibiotics but **higher doses and longer courses** — usually **about 2 weeks** — chosen from previous sputum results
Oral **ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg twice daily** (Kumar: 750 mg bd), or IV antipseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime); dual therapy if multi-resistant
Eradication attempt, then long-term **nebulised colistimethate or an aminoglycoside**

blocks.text: US quick sources give an **empirical respiratory fluoroquinolone** when no culture is available. Davidson and Kumar instead **guide therapy by previous sputum microbiology**; Kumar adds that routine rotating antibiotics are no longer advised and **long-term quinolones should be avoided**.

blocks.title: Supportive measures
items: Smoking cessation; annual **influenza** and **pneumococcal** vaccination.
Bronchodilators (β2-agonist and/or antimuscarinic) can ease symptoms even when FEV1 does not change; inhaled corticosteroids help some patients.
**Pulmonary rehabilitation** for reduced exercise capacity and breathlessness.
Respiratory failure: oxygen and **non-invasive ventilation**; refer suitable patients for **lung transplantation**.
ABPA: systemic glucocorticoid plus an azole (itraconazole or voriconazole) ± omalizumab.

blocks.title: Haemoptysis
rows: Usually settles once the infection is treated
Admit; protect the airway and resuscitate; **bleeding side down**; oxygen, large-bore IV access, bloods incl. clotting, ABG, CXR; early respiratory and thoracic surgical referral
**Bronchial artery embolisation**; surgery if embolisation fails

blocks.title: Surgery and prognosis
items: Resection suits only the **few** with disease **confined to one lobe or segment** on CT; many medical failures are unsuitable because disease is bilateral or airflow obstruction is severe.
Disease linked to **ciliary dysfunction or CF** progresses to respiratory failure; otherwise outlook can be fairly good with regular physiotherapy and vigorous antibiotic use.
**Low FEV1** and **P. aeruginosa infection** predict a worse outcome.
Prevention: protect children against **measles and whooping cough**, treat primary TB, and relieve bronchial obstruction early.

blocks.title: Complications to remember
items: Haemoptysis (may be massive), pneumonia, empyema, pneumothorax
Aspergillus and non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection
Metastatic **cerebral abscess**
Respiratory failure

blocks.text: **CF lung disease is managed as severe bronchiectasis**: daily physiotherapy; Staph. aureus can often be treated orally, but **Pseudomonas usually needs IV antibiotics**; resistant colonisers (P. aeruginosa, S. maltophilia, B. cepacia) may need unusual combinations.

**Suppurative pneumonia** destroys lung tissue through the inflammatory process. A **lung abscess** is a localised pocket of pus, or a cavity whose wall is chronic inflammatory tissue; on CXR or CT it appears as a **cavity, often with an air–fluid level**.

blocks.title: Causes and likely organisms
rows: **Aspiration** — ENT or dental surgery under anaesthesia, vomit during coma, alcoholism, bulbar or vocal cord palsy, achalasia/reflux, poor oral hygiene
Mixed mouth flora: **anaerobes plus aerobes** (Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, anaerobic cocci)
Pneumonia in a previously healthy lung
Tumour or foreign body — must be found and removed
**Injecting drug users** with tricuspid/pulmonary valve endocarditis (usually Staph. aureus)
Pulmonary infarction; infected emphysematous bulla; Lemierre syndrome (Fusobacterium necrophorum)

blocks.text: Aspiration settles in **dependent** lung: Davidson cites the apical segment of a lower lobe in a supine patient; Kumar & Clark Essentials says it usually enters the **right lower lobe (posterior segment)**, reflecting bronchial anatomy. Anaerobes are common, so cover them (metronidazole).

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: Pneumonia that **persists or worsens** despite treatment.
Cough with **large amounts of foul-smelling sputum** (anaerobes), sometimes blood-stained.
Sudden expectoration of a large volume of foul pus when the abscess **ruptures into a bronchus**.
**High swinging (remittent) fever**, marked malaise and weight loss.
**Clubbing** — can appear within **10–14 days**; pleural rub is common.

blocks.title: Investigations
items: CXR/CT: cavity with fluid level; CT is essential to define it.
Bloods: normocytic anaemia and raised inflammatory markers.
Microbiology from sputum, **bronchoscopy**, transtracheal or percutaneous aspiration.
Bronchoscopy also **excludes carcinoma and foreign body** and can remove an obstructing object.

blocks.title: Treatment
items: Antibiotics covering **aerobes and anaerobes**: Davidson — **amoxicillin + metronidazole**; Kumar & Clark Essentials — IV cefuroxime + metronidazole for 5 days, then oral therapy.
Courses are long: **4–6 weeks** may be needed for an abscess.
**Physiotherapy/postural drainage** is valuable, especially for lower-lobe disease or large cavities.
Remove or treat any obstructing endobronchial lesion; **surgery** if no improvement despite optimal medical therapy.
Empyema (abscess rupture into the pleura) needs prompt chest drainage.

blocks.text: Most patients respond well, but **residual fibrosis and bronchiectasis are common sequelae**. An abscess that fails to resolve should prompt bronchoscopy to look for an **obstructing carcinoma**.

cards.back: Permanent abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with chronic suppurative airway infection, daily sputum and progressive scarring.

cards.front: Can the chest examination be normal in bronchiectasis?
cards.back: Yes — if the dilated airways are empty of secretions and there is no collapse, there may be no signs.

cards.front: Haemoptysis + finger clubbing: two diagnoses to think of first?

cards.back: Primary ciliary dyskinesia with sinusitis and situs inversus (dextrocardia), causing bronchiectasis.
Acquired mucociliary clearance defect: bronchiectasis with sinusitis and azoospermia.

cards.front: CF: inheritance, gene location, commonest mutation?
cards.back: Autosomal recessive; CFTR on the long arm of chromosome 7; ΔF508.
Non-tapering thick-walled "tram-track" airways; bronchus larger than its accompanying artery (signet ring sign).

cards.front: Which bronchiectasis patients need a sweat test and CF genetics?
cards.back: Everyone under 40, and any age if suspicion is high.

cards.front: Screening tests for primary ciliary dyskinesia?
cards.back: Nasal nitric oxide (very low) and the saccharin test (normally tasted within 20 min; prolonged in PCD).

cards.front: Oral antibiotic for P. aeruginosa in bronchiectasis?
cards.back: Ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg twice daily (IV alternative: piperacillin–tazobactam or ceftazidime).

cards.front: Long-term drug that reduces bronchiectasis exacerbations?
Massive haemoptysis: definition and definitive treatment?
cards.back: > 200 mL in 24 h; airway protection and resuscitation, then bronchial artery embolisation (surgery if it fails).

cards.front: First-line antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia / lung abscess (Davidson)?
cards.back: Amoxicillin plus metronidazole; an abscess may need 4–6 weeks.

cards.front: Lung abscess in an injecting drug user — mechanism?
cards.back: Haematogenous spread (septic emboli) from tricuspid/pulmonary valve endocarditis.

cards.front: How fast can clubbing develop in suppurative pneumonia?

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has coughed every day for 12 years. She brings up about a cupful of green sputum each morning, has had repeated chest infections, and her partner complains of bad breath. She has never smoked. She has finger clubbing and coarse crackles at both lung bases.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Daily copious purulent sputum, halitosis, recurrent infections, coarse crackles and clubbing are the classic cluster for **bronchiectasis**.
whyNot: A never-smoker with large daily volumes of purulent sputum and clubbing does not fit COPD.
Asthma gives variable wheeze and breathlessness, not daily purulent sputum or clubbing.
IPF causes a dry cough with fine basal crackles, not copious green sputum.
Sarcoidosis usually causes a dry cough and hilar nodes; clubbing and purulent sputum are not typical.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with known bronchiectasis presents with an infective exacerbation. His dilated lower-lobe airways are full of secretions.
questions.leadIn: Which auscultatory finding is most expected over the affected lobes?
options: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds
questions.explanation: When the bronchiectatic spaces hold a lot of sputum, **numerous coarse crackles** are heard over the affected areas, usually basally.
whyNot: Fine "velcro" crackles suggest pulmonary fibrosis.
Absent breath sounds with hyper-resonance suggest a pneumothorax.
Stony dullness suggests a pleural effusion.
A pericardial rub is a cardiac sign and unrelated to airway secretions.

questions.stem: A medical student is preparing a talk on the global burden of bronchiectasis.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which is the commonest cause of bronchiectasis worldwide?
questions.explanation: Both Davidson and Kumar state that **TB is the leading cause worldwide**. A US review book names CF, but that reflects a US case mix.
whyNot: CF is a major cause in some Western series, but not worldwide; Kumar treats CF bronchiectasis as a separate entity.
PCD is a rare congenital cause.
ABPA is a recognised but much less common cause, seen mainly in asthma or CF.
Antibody deficiency is an uncommon cause.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has had a productive cough since early childhood and chronic sinusitis. He and his partner are attending a fertility clinic. Examination finds the apex beat in the right fifth intercostal space. HRCT shows bronchiectasis.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sinusitis, bronchiectasis and infertility point to a ciliary problem; the **right-sided apex (dextrocardia)** marks **Kartagener syndrome**, a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia.
whyNot: CF causes infertility through failed vas deferens development, but not situs inversus.
Young syndrome combines sinusitis and azoospermia but with normal anatomy.
Antibody deficiency does not cause dextrocardia or infertility.
ABPA occurs in asthma or CF and does not cause situs inversus.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a chronic productive cough and recurrent chest infections. His chest X-ray is reported as normal.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is the investigation of choice to confirm bronchiectasis?
questions.explanation: **HRCT** is the investigation of choice (gold standard). It shows non-tapering thick-walled airways and the signet ring sign; the CXR is often normal.
whyNot: A plain film is insensitive; repeating it adds little.
Bronchoscopy looks for local obstruction or samples, but does not show the airway dilatation.
Spirometry may show obstruction but cannot confirm bronchiectasis.
Culture guides antibiotics but does not establish the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has newly diagnosed bronchiectasis on HRCT. She has no history of severe childhood infection, TB or asthma.
questions.leadIn: Which test should be performed in every patient with bronchiectasis in her age group?
options: Sweat test with CF genetic analysis
Nasal biopsy for ciliary electron microscopy
questions.explanation: Kumar recommends a **sweat test and CF genetic assessment for all patients under 40**, and at any age when suspicion is high.
whyNot: Ciliary biopsy is a specialist second step after screening (e.g. nasal NO) suggests PCD.
Serum ACE relates to sarcoidosis, not routine bronchiectasis work-up.
A V/Q scan looks for pulmonary embolism.
Angiography is used to treat massive haemoptysis, not for aetiology.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has a two-week exacerbation with more purulent sputum. All her sputum cultures over the past year have grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She is well enough for oral treatment.
questions.leadIn: Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For Pseudomonas, Davidson recommends **oral ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg twice daily** (or an IV antipseudomonal β-lactam if oral therapy is unsuitable). Courses are longer than for COPD — usually about 2 weeks.
whyNot: Amoxicillin does not cover P. aeruginosa; it suits H. influenzae.
Doxycycline does not cover P. aeruginosa.
Flucloxacillin is for Staph. aureus.
Clarithromycin is not an antipseudomonal agent.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has bronchiectasis confined to the right middle lobe on CT, with frequent exacerbations despite daily physiotherapy and appropriate antibiotics. His spirometry is near normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Surgical resection of the affected lobe
questions.explanation: Surgery helps the small group with **disease limited to one lobe or segment** who fail medical treatment and have adequate lung function.
whyNot: Transplant is for severe, diffuse disease with respiratory failure.
Kumar advises avoiding long-term quinolones.
Routine rotating antibiotic regimens are no longer recommended.
Embolisation treats significant haemoptysis, not recurrent infection.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with heavy alcohol use was found unconscious after a binge two weeks ago. He now has a swinging fever, cough with foul-tasting sputum and weight loss. His chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity with an air–fluid level.
questions.leadIn: Which organisms are most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Loss of consciousness with alcohol → **aspiration** of mouth flora → abscess with a **mixture of anaerobes and aerobes**, hence the foul sputum.
whyNot: TB cavitates but rarely with an acute aspiration history and foul sputum; it would still need excluding.
Pseudomonas is typical of established bronchiectasis/CF, not aspiration abscess.
Pneumocystis affects the immunocompromised and causes diffuse shadowing.
Legionella causes a severe pneumonia, not a classic aspiration abscess.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who injects heroin has fever and rigors. A new pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge increases on inspiration. Chest CT shows several cavitating nodules scattered through both lungs.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of his lung lesions?
questions.explanation: Injecting drug users are prone to **haematogenous lung abscess** with **tricuspid valve endocarditis**; multiple bilateral cavitating lesions fit seeding from the blood.
whyNot: Aspiration usually gives a single abscess in a dependent segment.
TB is not suggested by the acute course and murmur.
Carcinoma causes a single localised obstruction, not multiple nodules with a murmur.
Infected bullae give a cavity with fluid level in an emphysematous lung, not multiple nodules.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis asks why her airway mucus is so thick.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains her airway disease?
options: Reduced chloride secretion with excess sodium and water absorption
Absent dynein arms in the cilia
questions.explanation: Defective **CFTR** reduces chloride secretion and removes inhibition of epithelial sodium channels, so sodium and water are over-absorbed and the airway surface liquid becomes dehydrated.
whyNot: Dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia.
IgA deficiency causes bronchiectasis through poor immunity, not ion transport.
This describes ABPA, which can complicate CF but is not its basic defect.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with cystic fibrosis had Staph. aureus in his sputum throughout childhood. Over the last few years his lung function has fallen steadily.
questions.leadIn: Which organism most commonly colonises adults with cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Staph. aureus predominates in childhood; in adulthood **many patients become colonised with P. aeruginosa** (or S. maltophilia and other Gram-negative bacilli).
whyNot: Pneumococcus causes acute community pneumonia, not chronic CF colonisation.
Mycoplasma is an atypical pneumonia organism.
Legionella is acquired from water systems and causes acute pneumonia.
Psittacosis is linked to birds.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with long-standing bronchiectasis coughs up about 300 mL of fresh blood over 12 hours. He is resuscitated and his airway is secured.
questions.leadIn: What is the definitive first-line procedure to stop the bleeding?
questions.explanation: Massive haemoptysis is a life-threatening emergency. After airway protection, **bronchial artery embolisation** controls bleeding from the hypertrophied bronchial arteries; surgery is used if it fails.
whyNot: Bleeding in bronchiectasis comes from the bronchial, not the pulmonary, circulation.
Transplant is a long-term option for end-stage disease, not acute bleeding.
Hypertonic saline aids clearance and does not stop bleeding.
Azithromycin reduces exacerbations but has no role in acute haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with right-sided bronchiectasis has brisk haemoptysis. Bronchoscopy confirms bleeding from the right lower lobe while you wait for interventional radiology.
questions.leadIn: How should she be positioned?
options: Head-down tilt on her left side
questions.explanation: Keep the **bleeding side down** so blood does not spill into, and flood, the healthy lung.
whyNot: Left side down would drain blood into the good lung.
Supine allows blood to spread to both lungs.
Prone makes airway management hard and protects neither lung.
This positions the bleeding lung uppermost, as for postural drainage — the opposite of what is needed.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with asthma for 15 years has needed several courses of oral steroids this year. He coughs up brown mucus plugs. His eosinophil count is raised, and HRCT shows central bronchiectasis.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most useful to confirm the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Asthma with plugs, eosinophilia and bronchiectasis suggests **ABPA**; confirm with **Aspergillus-specific IgE (or skin-prick test) and total IgE**.
whyNot: Sweat testing is for CF.
Nasal NO screens for primary ciliary dyskinesia.
IgG subclasses look for antibody deficiency.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema rather than asthma with mucus plugs.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with idiopathic bronchiectasis has had four exacerbations needing antibiotics in the past year despite good daily airway clearance.
questions.leadIn: Which long-term drug is recommended to reduce her exacerbation frequency?
questions.explanation: **Long-term azithromycin** has an immunomodulatory effect and reduces exacerbations.
whyNot: Kumar warns that long-term quinolones should be avoided.
Long-term oral steroids are not a standard way to prevent exacerbations here.
Montelukast is an asthma drug.
Theophylline is a bronchodilator without proven benefit on exacerbations here.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man had dental extraction under general anaesthesia. Three weeks later he has a cough with foul sputum and fever; CXR shows a cavity with a fluid level in the right lower lobe.
questions.leadIn: Which initial antibiotic regimen is most appropriate according to Davidson?
questions.explanation: Aspiration abscess involves **aerobes and anaerobes**; **amoxicillin + metronidazole** usually suffices, and an abscess may need **4–6 weeks**.
whyNot: Flucloxacillin covers Staph. aureus but not anaerobes.
Anti-TB therapy is not indicated without evidence of TB.
Aminoglycosides do not cover anaerobes.
A macrolide alone gives poor anaerobic cover.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has bronchiectasis, chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent ear infections. Her heart and abdominal organs are normally positioned. A saccharin pellet placed in her anterior nose has still not been tasted after 60 minutes, and her nasal nitric oxide is very low.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A saccharin time far beyond **20 minutes** and **very low nasal NO** point to defective cilia — **primary ciliary dyskinesia**. Situs inversus (Kartagener) is present in only some patients.
whyNot: CF is diagnosed by sweat test and genetics; a prolonged saccharin time with very low nasal NO points instead to a primary ciliary defect.
Antibody deficiency does not slow mucociliary transit.
ABPA occurs with asthma or CF and does not affect ciliary transit.
Post-infective damage does not explain ear and sinus involvement or abnormal ciliary tests.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old ex-smoker presents with three episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has had a daily cough with large amounts of purulent sputum since severe whooping cough as a child. He has clubbing and coarse crackles at the left base.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his haemoptysis?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — haemoptysis + clubbing narrows the field to **lung cancer or bronchiectasis**. Step 2 — a **lifelong daily purulent cough beginning after whooping cough** is the typical story of post-infective bronchiectasis. Step 3 — coarse basal crackles fit secretions in dilated airways. Note that as an ex-smoker with clubbing he still needs cancer excluded, but the best single explanation is **bronchiectasis**.
whyNot: PE causes acute pleuritic pain and breathlessness, not decades of purulent sputum or clubbing.
Mitral stenosis gives breathlessness with a diastolic murmur; clubbing is not a feature.
Anti-GBM disease causes pulmonary haemorrhage with kidney involvement, not chronic sputum.
Acute bronchitis is short-lived and does not cause clubbing.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had recurrent sinus and chest infections since childhood. HRCT shows bilateral bronchiectasis. Sweat test is normal. Serum IgG is very low, and he fails to make antibodies after pneumococcal and tetanus vaccination.
questions.leadIn: What is the underlying cause of his bronchiectasis?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — bronchiectasis in a young adult → look for a cause (CF, ciliary, immune, ABPA). Step 2 — normal sweat test makes CF unlikely. Step 3 — **low IgG with failed vaccine responses** shows he cannot make protective antibody, so repeated bacterial infection damaged the bronchi: **primary hypogammaglobulinaemia**, listed by Davidson as a congenital cause.
whyNot: A normal sweat test makes CF unlikely.
Ciliary disease does not lower IgG or abolish vaccine responses.
ABPA causes high IgE in asthma or CF, not low IgG.
Young syndrome involves azoospermia with normal immunoglobulins.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old smoker develops right upper lobe pneumonia that cavitates. After three weeks of appropriate antibiotics the cavity and fever persist. He has no aspiration risk factors.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — a cavity with persisting fever is a **lung abscess**. Step 2 — an abscess that fails to respond, in a **smoker without aspiration risk**, raises suspicion of **bronchial obstruction by a tumour** (or a foreign body). Step 3 — **bronchoscopy** both samples the infection and excludes carcinoma or foreign body; any obstructing lesion must be treated.
whyNot: Sweat testing is for suspected CF in younger patients.
Nasal NO screens for ciliary dyskinesia.
Immunoglobulins are part of bronchiectasis work-up, not a non-resolving abscess in a smoker.
A V/Q scan looks for embolism.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of bronchiectasis from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has had bronchiectasis since childhood, worst in the upper lobes. He has had pale, floating stools since infancy, and his sputum, which grew Staph. aureus when he was young, now grows Pseudomonas.
items.explanation: Upper-lobe bronchiectasis from childhood, malabsorption and the Staph. aureus → Pseudomonas progression are typical of **cystic fibrosis**.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with asthma for 20 years finds it increasingly hard to control. He coughs up brownish plugs, his blood eosinophils are raised, and HRCT shows dilated central airways.
items.explanation: Two steps: difficult asthma with mucus plugs and eosinophilia → Aspergillus hypersensitivity; central bronchiectasis is its complication → **ABPA**.

items.stem: A thin 72-year-old non-smoking woman has a chronic cough which she tends to stifle and has lost weight. She has never had tuberculosis. CT shows bronchiectasis, tree-in-bud change and small nodules in the right middle lobe and lingula, and three sputum samples are positive for acid-fast bacilli.
items.explanation: Acid-fast bacilli with right middle lobe/lingula bronchiectasis in an older woman who suppresses her cough, and no previous TB → **NTM (MAC), "Lady Windermere" pattern**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man who grew up in a high-prevalence country was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 20 years ago. He now has recurrent haemoptysis and purulent sputum, and CT shows upper-lobe bronchiectasis with fibrosis.
items.explanation: Previous pulmonary TB with upper-lobe scarring → **post-tuberculous bronchiectasis**, the commonest cause worldwide.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with long-standing bronchiectasis has a chest X-ray.
questions.leadIn: Which plain film appearance is most consistent with bronchiectasis?
options: Kerley B lines at the costophrenic angles
questions.explanation: Thick-walled dilated airways appear as **tram-track lines** (side-on) and **ring shadows** (end-on). Many CXRs are normal, so CT is still needed.
whyNot: Kerley B lines indicate interstitial oedema.
Bat's-wing shadowing suggests pulmonary oedema.
Isolated hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
Miliary nodules suggest miliary TB.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with moderate bronchiectasis has lung function tests.
questions.leadIn: Which spirometric pattern is most typical?
options: Obstructive, with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
Restrictive, with a raised FEV1/FVC ratio
Normal volumes with an isolated low DLCO
Fixed upper-airway obstruction on the flow–volume loop
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis behaves as an **obstructive** airway disease: FEV1/FVC is reduced.
whyNot: A restrictive pattern suggests interstitial or chest wall disease.
An isolated low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease.
Fixed upper-airway obstruction comes from tracheal or laryngeal narrowing.
Spirometry may be normal in mild disease but obstruction is the typical pattern.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has increased purulent sputum. Her previous sputum cultures have repeatedly grown Haemophilus influenzae only, and she has no allergies.
questions.leadIn: Which oral antibiotic is the most appropriate first choice?
questions.explanation: H. influenzae is common in bronchiectasis and usually responds to **oral amoxicillin**, co-amoxiclav or doxycycline, chosen from previous cultures.
whyNot: Quinolones are kept for Pseudomonas; overuse should be avoided.
Nebulised colistimethate is for chronic Pseudomonas.
IV antipseudomonal therapy is unnecessary for sensitive H. influenzae.
Flucloxacillin targets Staph. aureus.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with non-CF bronchiectasis has had Pseudomonas aeruginosa in every sputum sample for two years, despite an eradication attempt. He has frequent exacerbations.
questions.leadIn: Which long-term antibiotic strategy is recommended?
questions.explanation: Borrowing from CF practice, chronic Pseudomonas is suppressed with **nebulised colistimethate or an aminoglycoside**.
whyNot: Long-term quinolones should be avoided.
Rotating oral antibiotic regimens are no longer recommended routinely.
Flucloxacillin does not cover Pseudomonas.
Amoxicillin does not cover Pseudomonas.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is being treated for a right lower lobe abscess. During a coughing fit he suddenly brings up a large amount of foul-smelling pus, after which his fever begins to settle.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Rupture of the abscess into a bronchus
Rupture of the abscess into the pleural space
Massive haemoptysis from a bronchial artery
questions.explanation: Sudden expectoration of copious foul sputum is the hallmark of an abscess **draining into a bronchus**.
whyNot: Rupture into the pleura produces an empyema, with worsening illness and no sudden sputum.
Infarction causes pleuritic pain and haemoptysis, not pus.
Pneumothorax causes sudden breathlessness, not purulent sputum.
He coughed up pus, not blood.

questions.stem: Two patients have bronchiectasis of similar extent on CT.
questions.leadIn: Which factor is associated with a poorer outcome?
options: Disease limited to a single segment
questions.explanation: Kumar notes that a **low FEV1** and **P. aeruginosa infection** predict a worse prognosis.
whyNot: H. influenzae is common and usually responds to oral antibiotics; it is not named as an adverse factor.
Localised disease is the group suitable for surgical resection.
A low, not normal, FEV1 is the adverse factor.
Regular physiotherapy improves outlook.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis. He has had no children despite trying for several years and semen analysis shows azoospermia. His sweat test and CF genetics are normal, and his heart is on the left.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Young syndrome** is an acquired mucociliary clearance defect with **sinusitis and azoospermia**; normal sweat test and normal anatomy argue against CF and Kartagener.
whyNot: Kartagener syndrome includes situs inversus; his heart is normally placed.
Normal sweat test and genetics make CF very unlikely.
Antibody deficiency does not cause azoospermia.
ABPA occurs in asthma or CF and does not cause infertility.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 33-year-old woman with no risk factors for aspiration develops a severe pneumonia that cavitates within a week.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: When suppurative pneumonia or abscess arises in a **previously healthy lung**, Davidson names **Staph. aureus or Klebsiella pneumoniae** as the usual causes.
whyNot: Mycoplasma causes an atypical pneumonia that rarely cavitates.
Pneumocystis affects the immunocompromised and gives diffuse shadowing.
Legionella causes severe pneumonia but is not a typical cause of abscess.
Psittacosis follows bird exposure and does not typically cavitate.

questions.stem: A public health team wants to reduce the number of children who later develop bronchiectasis.
questions.leadIn: Which measure does Davidson emphasise?
options: Childhood immunisation against measles and whooping cough
Annual screening chest X-rays in children
Inhaled corticosteroids for all children with cough
Routine sweat testing of all adults
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis often starts after **measles, whooping cough or primary TB** in childhood, so preventing and treating these — plus early relief of bronchial obstruction — is the key preventive step.
whyNot: CXR is insensitive and screening does not prevent disease.
Antibiotics for viral colds do not prevent bronchiectasis.
Inhaled steroids do not prevent post-infective damage.
Sweat testing detects CF; it does not prevent bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with cystic fibrosis asks why he and his partner have been unable to conceive.
questions.leadIn: What is the usual cause of infertility in men with CF?
options: Failure of development of the vas deferens
Immotile sperm due to dynein arm defects
questions.explanation: Most men with CF are infertile because the **vas deferens fails to develop**; sperm can be retrieved surgically for IVF.
whyNot: Dynein defects belong to primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Sperm are produced and can be retrieved surgically, so testicular failure is not the usual cause.
Pituitary function is not the problem in CF.
Retrograde ejaculation occurs after prostate surgery or in diabetic neuropathy.

questions.stem: A saccharin test is performed to screen a patient with bronchiectasis for ciliary dysfunction.
questions.leadIn: What is the upper limit of normal for tasting the saccharin?
questions.explanation: The pellet should reach the pharynx and be tasted within **20 minutes**; the time is greatly prolonged in ciliary dysfunction. Nasal biopsy (beat frequency, electron microscopy) confirms.
whyNot: Far too short; normal transit takes longer than this.
Too short to be the threshold.
A time this long would be abnormal.
A time this long would be abnormal.

ospe.identify: Finger clubbing (front and side views): lost angle at the nail fold and increased nail curvature. In a respiratory patient, think of chronic suppuration (bronchiectasis, abscess, empyema, CF) or lung cancer.
CT chest: dilated bronchi with thickened walls in both lower lobes, which means bronchiectasis.
CT: each thick-walled bronchus is wider than its neighbouring artery (signet ring sign), which means bronchiectasis.
CT in cystic fibrosis: markedly dilated, thick-walled airways, which is bronchiectasis.
Diagram of the CF epithelial defect: faulty apical CFTR chloride channel, uninhibited sodium channel, excess sodium and water absorption, dehydrated airway lining.
